Autoresearch

Turn Claude Code, OpenCode, OpenAI Codex, pi, or Muse into an engine that won't stop improving.

Karpathy's autoresearch, in one line: constraint plus a mechanical metric plus autonomous iteration equals compounding gains.

"Set the GOAL → The agent runs the LOOP → You wake up to results"

You don't need AGI. You need a goal, a metric, and a loop that never quits.

The core skill, bundled runtime, installation, and verification run on Claude Code, OpenCode, OpenAI Codex, pi, and Muse. Hook guardrails ship for Claude Code (native hooks) and pi (extension events).

Fork-and-flush: metric loops escape plateaus the way Cai et al. (arXiv:2610.07447) do. At 33% and 66% of the budget, or after 5 iterations with no keep, the loop forks fresh-context branches from the best commit so far, runs each briefly, and keeps the winner. Half the branches pick their own ideas (randomness); the other half each get a distinct experiment from a stateless Advisor that reads the results log (Zhang et al., arXiv:2610.07625); Guided: R sets the split. The orchestrator answers a plateau with FORK before it gives up. See guide/autoresearch.md.

SkillsBench is a benchmark that tests whether AI agents can use Skills to complete professional tasks across many domains. The point is to measure how much a model's ability to solve complex real-world tasks improves when it has specialized Skills available.

To test performance in production-like environments where many Skills are installed at once, we adapted SkillsBench into a large-scale multi-Skill setting. In the original SkillsBench setup, each task comes with only the specialized Skill for that task. In our modified setting, every task is evaluated in a global environment containing all 195 specialized Skills, and all other experimental conditions stay the same. The goal is to see whether an agent can find, select, and orchestrate the right Skills from a large installed pool on its own, and organize them into a workflow that completes complex tasks.

We benchmarked vibeskills v4.1.0 on SkillsBench using DeepSeekV4Flash-VE and OpenHands as the baseline evaluation setup. Compared with the baseline without vibeskills, vibeskills raised the mean verifier reward by 21.12 percentage points, cut token consumption by 29.6%, and reduced tool calls by 33.1%.

Bumblebee

Bumblebee collects package, extension, and developer-tool metadata from macOS and Linux developer endpoints. It reads. It never writes.

Here's the question it answers: an advisory just dropped and names a package, extension, or version. Which of your developer machines have a match sitting in their on-disk metadata right now?

SBOMs tell you what shipped. EDR tells you what ran or touched the network. Neither helps when you need to see the messy local state on a developer machine: lockfiles, package-manager metadata, extension manifests, supported developer-tool configs.

Bumblebee reads that scattered state and turns it into structured NDJSON component records. Hand it an exposure catalog and it flags exact matches. If you already know what you're hunting, you get a fast, read-only exposure check. Nothing on disk changes.
